title: Who am I?
hookLine: a sixteen-year-old lies down as if dead and asks what's left
carry: i am not the body or the mind

lines: HE LIES DOWN AS IF DEAD.
cards: Madurai, south India, 1896. A sixteen-year-old schoolboy named Venkataraman is alone in his uncle's house when a sudden fear of death comes over him. He isn't ill.
Instead of calling for help, he lies down, stretches out stiff the way a body lies, holds his breath, and asks himself: this body is dead. They'll carry it off and burn it. But am I dead?
And he finds, by his own later account, that something is still here, aware, untouched. A few weeks later he leaves home for a holy hill called Arunachala, and stays there for the rest of his life.
The world knows him as Ramana Maharshi.

teach.b: Years later at Arunachala, when tradition says he hardly spoke, a visitor brought him questions, and the answers came back written down. They became a little text called Who Am I?

It starts where everyone can check: every being wants to be happy and not to suffer. Happiness, Ramana says, is our real nature, and to find it we need to know ourselves. The way to know yourself is to ask: who am I?
The answer moves by taking things away. The body is not I. The senses are not I.
The breath is not I. Even the mind, the thing that thinks, is not I. If I am none of these, what am I?
What's left, the text says, is awareness, and that is what I am.

teach.h: NOT THE BODY, NOT THE SENSES, NOT THE MIND.
teach.b: This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings, the atman: your true self is not the body and not the mind.
The Upanishads walk this road, setting things aside as not this, not this, and Ramana walked it first, on his uncle's floor. Listen to ordinary speech: my hand, my thoughts, my mood.
Someone is doing the owning, and Ramana's question is aimed at that owner.

teach.h: WHAT REMAINS IS AWARENESS: THE ATMAN.
teach.b: So when a bad grade, a mirror or a rough mood tries to tell you who you are, this teaching says: that is something you notice, not what you are.
He doesn't ask you to believe it. He asks you to look.

how: People who follow Ramana's teaching practice self-inquiry, turning attention back to the sense of 'I' and asking 'who am I?'; Who Am I? is read and recited at his ashram at the foot of Arunachala in Tiruvannamalai and by readers around the world.

o: the sage of Arunachala who taught asking: who am I?
a teacher who said the thinking mind is the true self
a king who left his throne to live on a holy hill

games.q: Who Am I? — tap the pairs.
p: lay down as if dead: am I dead?
the body, senses, breath and mind

s: Ramana's turning point came when, at sixteen, he lay down as if dead and asked what was left
by his own account, he found something still aware and untouched, and soon left home for Arunachala.
Ramana says the thinking mind is the real I
even the mind is set aside as 'not I'. what remains is awareness.
Ramana asks the reader to accept his answer on faith
the question is meant to be looked into, not believed.

games.q: you've set aside the body, the senses, the breath and even your thoughts as 'not I'. what does Ramana say is left?
o: awareness, and that is what I am.
a soul shaped like the body.
games.why: in Who Am I?, after everything is set aside, awareness alone remains, and Ramana says that is the I.

practice: Notice the body's weight on the seat, then a sound in the room, then a thought passing, and say quietly to each: this is noticed.
Now turn gently toward whatever is doing the noticing and ask once, without hurry, who am I, resting your attention there without reaching for words, the way you'd rest your eyes on a far horizon.
If you pray, you can let that resting be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Ramana Maharshi. The teacher of Arunachala who, at sixteen, asked: am I dead? His little text Who Am I? sets down body, senses and mind, and asks what's left.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: vichara, inquiry. Ramana's way is often called atma-vichara, inquiry into the self.

carryVoice: Your line: i am not the body or the mind. Tomorrow, how to ask it when the thoughts won't stop. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

sources.ref: Ramana Maharshi's account of his death experience in Madurai, 1896, as recorded in B. V. Narasimha Swami, Self-Realization (1931), ch. on the awakening
sources.work: B. V. Narasimha Swami, Self-Realization: The Life and Teachings of Sri Ramana Maharshi (paraphrased)
